ENT CLINICAL NOTE

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  • 2–3-day history of wheeze and shortness of breath.  
  • No clear precipitant identified; clinician suggested possible pollen (hay-fever related) or viral trigger.

- Symptom timeline and progression:
  • Onset 2–3 days ago, persistent.  
  • Dyspnea on exertion; able to speak in full sentences at rest but occasionally “can’t finish sentences.”  
  • No nocturnal symptoms.

- ENT symptoms:
  • Throat swelling/closure sensation: Denied.  
  • Voice change/hoarseness: Denied.  
  • Dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling: Denied.  
  • Nasal/ocular: History of hay fever; no acute nasal/ocular complaints reported.  
  • Stridor/noisy breathing: Denied; wheeze described as chest-based.  
  • Dyspnea: Present on exertion only.  
  • Swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face): None.  
  • Ear or neck symptoms: None.

- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  • Childhood asthma—severe enough to require occasional hospital visits but no ICU admissions.  
  • Last regular asthma medication use reportedly stopped 3–4 years ago (see conflict).  
  • Current rescue therapy: Salbutamol inhaler. No previous adrenaline/epinephrine use or ED visits for current episode.

- Allergies and current medications:
  • Drug/food allergies: None known.  
  • Medications:  
    – Salbutamol inhaler, dose/route/frequency not documented (patient reports use every few weeks; instructed to increase temporarily).  
    – No regular antihistamine; to start OTC antihistamine (agent/dose not documented).

- Social context:
  • Lives with partner; works as an engineer, currently working from home/sick leave.  
  • Non-smoker; drinks ~1 glass of wine every 2–3 days.

Objective:
- Observable swelling: Not reported.  
- Airway/breathing: Wheeze described by patient; no stridor; breathing comfortable at rest.  
- Mental status: Alert; no dizziness or syncope reported.  
- Vitals/ENT examination: Temperature self-checked at 37 °C; no other vitals recorded.  
- Presence of another person: Partner at home (not present during call).

Assessment:
- Likely asthma exacerbation (mild–moderate) with dyspnea on exertion in a patient with childhood-onset asthma and current salbutamol use; possible allergic (pollen) or viral trigger.  
- No red-flag ENT airway symptoms (no throat swelling, stridor, or facial/oral edema).  
- Conflict noted: Patient initially stated cessation of inhaler 3–4 years ago but later reported “normally” using salbutamol every few weeks.

Plan:
- Medications/devices:
  • Prescribe peak-flow meter for home monitoring.  
  • Prescribe spacer device; pharmacist to demonstrate technique.  
  • Salbutamol: Increase to 2–4 puffs every 4 hours as needed (dose/route/frequency otherwise per current inhaler instructions).  
  • Start regular oral antihistamine (OTC; specific agent/dose not documented).

- Monitoring/education:
  • Record peak-flow readings morning and evening for one week.  
  • Maintain log of symptoms and inhaler use.

- Escalation / red-flags:
  • Seek immediate medical attention (call emergency services) for any of the following:  
    – Worsening breathlessness at rest or inability to speak full sentences.  
    – Appearance of throat tightness, voice change, stridor, or any facial/oral swelling.  
    – Peak-flow dropping to personal best <50 % once established.  
    – New high fever or chest pain.

- Follow-up:
  • Telephone/virtual review in 1 week with peak-flow diary to consider additional controller therapy.  
  • Instructed to contact clinic sooner if symptoms worsen despite increased salbutamol.

Quality checks (document_quality):
• Missing but expected elements:
  – Objective lung and ENT examination findings (auscultation, oropharynx).  
  – Full vital signs (RR, HR, BP, O₂ saturation).  
  – Exact salbutamol dose and formulation.  
  – Specific antihistamine name/dose.  
  – Personal best peak-flow baseline.  
  – Documentation of inhaled corticosteroid consideration or allergy/asthma action plan.

• Internal conflicts:
  – Patient stated discontinuing inhalers 3–4 years ago but later described usual salbutamol use every few weeks.

• Transcript quality:
  – Clear overall; occasional short pauses and minor ambiguities but no major audio gaps.
